newsitem.title: USA: IMM currency futures mixed, marks rise on U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: IMM currency futures mixed, marks rise on U.S. data.

text.p: IMM currency futures were mixed, with marks rising slightly on the decline in the U.S. February Producer Price Index (PPI), traders and analysts said.
June marks held losses above major support at $0.5882, or about 1.71 spot marks, and tested resistance at $0.5906, which is roughly equivalent to dollar/mark's early morning decline to 1.7030 spot.
The overall PPI fell 0.4 percent, compared to average trade estimates for a decline of 0.1 percent, and dampened expectations for higher U.S. rates at the end of the month.
Core PPI, which excludes food and energy prices, was down 0.1 percent, against estimates for up 0.1 percent. January PPI figures were unrevised.
Traders said some currency futures had an immediate positive response to the data, which lifted U.S. T-bond futures.
"As bonds went up, U.S. yields drifted lower and that helped currencies," one floor trader said. June yen temporarily trimmed losses.
However, one desk trader said U.S. bonds should have rallied much sharper after the data.
"You are obviously at a threshold at whether or not there is a rate hike," Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney, said.

An article in Friday's Washington Post suggested that it was not yet clear whether the surprising strength in the U.S. economy will cause the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise short-term rates on March 25.
"Yes, but then you have Moskow's comments hanging over our heads," another floor trader said, referring to Chicago Federal Reserve bank president Michael Moskow's comments late Thursday.
Moskow said that the Fed must have a preemptive policy to head off inflation pressures.
Finstrom also said the dollar was benefiting slightly from the flows out of European currencies, including the mark, on concerns about the fate of the European Monetary Union (EMU).
The currency futures pits have been rife with speculation that Europe will announce a delay in the EMU.
While the speculation has kept marks well bid against many cash crosses, the general European angst about growth and labor has supported the dollar.
Most currency futures turned higher in a knee-jerk reaction to a wire-service story reporting that U.S. Treasury secretary Robert Rubin will draw the line at a dollar/yen level of 130.00 spot.

At 0953 CST/1553 GMT, June yen was down $0.000006 at $0.008202, marks were up $0.0023 at $0.5915, Swiss francs were up $0.0022 at $0.6904, sterling was up $0.0042 at $1.5984, Canadian dollars were up $0.0005 at $0.7377, Australian dollars were $0.0040 higher at $0.7965 and Mexican pesos were up $0.000400 at $0.119950.
